# Embeddings and Representation Learning {#sec-embeddings}

An embedding model is a versioned scoring interface. It turns text, its role
(query or document), and an optional task instruction into a fixed-length
vector, the embedding. A retrieval system can then compare one query vector
with millions of stored document vectors without running a language model over
every pair. The interface promises only that text pairs judged relevant by the
training process should receive higher scores than irrelevant pairs. Nearness
does not by itself mean that two texts are synonyms, factually correct,
authorized for the same user, or useful for every task.

Chapter @sec-rag-retrieval treated dense retrieval, the vector comparison just
described, as one candidate-generation channel. This chapter describes how that
channel is built. The engineering problem is to define one scoring contract,
meaning the recorded choices that fix how text becomes a vector and how two
vectors are scored, then learn a model that satisfies it from imperfect pairs,
preserve it through indexing, and detect when a model or index change has
broken it.

## Start with the scoring contract

An embedding has meaning only together with the transformation that produced
it. Two arrays of 768 floating-point numbers are not necessarily comparable.
They may come from different tokenizers, pooling rules (how per-token states
become one vector), task prompts, model checkpoints, or normalization
conventions. Record those choices as data:

```text
EmbeddingSpec {
  model_id, model_revision, tokenizer_revision
  query_role, document_role, instruction_version
  pooling, source_layer, max_tokens, truncation_policy
  dimension, normalization, similarity, dtype, quantization
}

EmbeddingRecord {
  tenant, document_id, chunk_id, source_version, content_hash
  embedding_spec_hash, vector, acl_version, index_generation
}
```

The spec is part of the index schema. A query must use a compatible query-side
spec, and every stored vector must use the corresponding document-side spec.
For an asymmetric retrieval model, those two roles may add different prefixes
or use different encoder weights. Omitting a required query instruction changes
the scoring function the model applies.

Let $E_q$ denote the query encoder and $E_d$ the document encoder, the functions
that map query text and document text to vectors. The pair is called a dual
encoder, and its two halves may share weights or be separate networks. For
query text $x$ and document text $y$, define

$$
u = E_q(x),
\qquad
v = E_d(y),
\qquad
s(x,y) = u^\mathsf{T}v.
$$

Here $u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are $d$-dimensional vectors,
$u^\mathsf{T}v$ is their inner product, and $s(x,y)$ is the score used for
ranking. If the contract applies $\ell_2$ normalization,

$$
\widehat{u}=\frac{u}{\lVert u\rVert_2},
\qquad
\widehat{v}=\frac{v}{\lVert v\rVert_2},
\qquad
\widehat{u}^{\mathsf{T}}\widehat{v}
= 1-\frac{1}{2}\lVert\widehat{u}-\widehat{v}\rVert_2^2.
$$

The hats denote unit-length vectors and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is Euclidean
norm. On unit vectors, cosine similarity, inner product, and squared Euclidean
distance induce the same ranking, with distance ordered in the opposite
direction. Without normalization, vector length affects the inner product.
Normalization must therefore match training and indexing; it is not a generic
post-processing improvement. Dense Passage Retrieval, for example, trained and
searched with an unnormalized inner product [@karpukhin2020dense].

## Pooling decides what one vector contains

A transformer produces one hidden state per input token, a vector that
represents that token in its context. Retrieval usually
needs one vector per query or chunk, so a pooling rule must compress those token
states. For masked mean pooling,

$$
z(x)=
\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} a_t h_t}
     {\sum_{t=1}^{T} a_t}.
$$

Here $x$ contains $T$ token positions, $h_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the hidden
state at position $t$, and $a_t\in\{0,1\}$ excludes padding or any other token
the contract says not to pool. A special-token pooler instead chooses one
$h_t$; max pooling takes a coordinate-wise maximum; learned attention assigns
data-dependent weights. The chosen layer, inclusion of special tokens, padding
mask, and normalization after pooling all affect the result.

Sentence-BERT combined extra training with a pooling interface of this kind. Its
siamese encoder, one network applied to each sentence of a pair, produced
sentence vectors that could be compared directly, avoiding pairwise BERT
inference for semantic search. Mean pooling was its default and worked well in
its reported ablations (runs that swap one component at a time), but that
experiment does not make mean pooling universal [@reimers2019sbert].
Decoder-based embedders may use the last token, bidirectional attention, or a
learned pooler. Those are separate designs, not stages in a single historical
progression. The causal mask a generator needs, under which each position attends
only to earlier ones, leaves early tokens blind to the rest of the text, so several
decoder-based embedders remove it. LLM2Vec converts a decoder in three unsupervised
steps: enable bidirectional attention, adapt with masked next-token prediction, then
train contrastively in the SimCSE style [@behnamghader2024llm2vec]. NV-Embed also
trains with bidirectional attention and replaces mean and last-token pooling with a
learned latent-attention layer [@lee2024nvembed].

Unadapted language-model states are not a retrieval metric by default. The
pretraining objective supervises token prediction and places no constraint on
how pooled query-document scores are ordered. Early contextual models also
exhibited anisotropy: randomly sampled token representations often had a
positive mean cosine rather than spreading evenly around the origin
[@ethayarajh2019contextual]. In GPT-2's last layer the average cosine between two
random token representations was close to 0.99, which leaves cosine similarity
almost no range to separate related from unrelated text. That result concerned contextual token occurrences
in particular BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2 checkpoints. It is a geometric warning, not
proof that anisotropy causes every pooling failure or that an isotropic space
must retrieve well. Later analyses found that correcting anisotropy alone does
not necessarily restore semantic isometry, the property that distances between
representations track differences in meaning [@fuster2022anisotropy]. The
operational test is still ranking quality on the intended query and corpus
distribution.

Two effects share the word "cone" and are easy to conflate. Representation
degeneration concerns the static token-embedding matrix: in a likelihood-trained
model with tied input and output embeddings, the softmax gradient for rare tokens
pushes their embeddings toward a shared direction [@gao2019degeneration].
Contextual anisotropy concerns per-token hidden states and appears in the
bidirectional BERT as well as in GPT-2, so autoregression alone does not explain it.
Post-hoc corrections spread the space from outside, by whitening the
representations [@su2021whitening] or mapping them to a Gaussian with a normalizing
flow [@li2020bertflow]. SimCSE's analysis found that these corrections improve
uniformity at the cost of alignment, both defined in the next section, while its
contrastive objective improved uniformity and kept alignment [@gao2021simcse].

## Contrastive learning shapes the ranking

Contrastive training writes the scoring contract into the training objective.
Its loss, the quantity the optimizer minimizes, shrinks as each labeled
relevant pair scores further above the other pairs it is compared against.
Suppose a batch has $B$ labeled pairs $(x_i,y_i)$, where $y_i$ is relevant to
query $x_i$. Let $u_i=E_q(x_i)$ and $v_j=E_d(y_j)$. A common in-batch loss for
query $i$ is

$$
\mathcal{L}_i
= -\log
\frac{\exp\!\left(s(u_i,v_i)/\tau\right)}
{\sum_{j=1}^{B}\exp\!\left(s(u_i,v_j)/\tau\right)}.
$$

Here $s$ is the similarity function the contract fixes, $v_i$ is the labeled
positive, the other $v_j$ are candidate negatives for query $i$, and $\tau>0$ is
the temperature, which scales scores before the softmax. The batch loss is
$B^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\mathcal{L}_i$. The softmax compares the positive only with
the particular negative set presented during training, a small sample of the
documents the model will meet in production.

This loss is known as InfoNCE and was introduced in contrastive predictive
coding [@oord2018cpc]. Under its specific sampling construction, one candidate
comes from the conditional distribution $p(d\mid q)$ and the others are
independent draws from the marginal $p(d)$. The expected objective then gives a
mutual-information lower bound whose ceiling grows as $\log B$. With an
unrestricted scorer, the optimal logit (the score inside the exponential)
differs by a query-only constant from $\log\!\left[p(d\mid q)/p(d)\right]$. If
negatives instead come from a mining proposal $\nu(d)$, the distribution of a
procedure that searches for hard negatives (documents not labeled relevant that
the current model scores highly), that ratio changes to $p(d\mid q)/\nu(d)$;
query-dependent hard mining may invalidate the standard mutual-information
interpretation entirely. More candidates raise the bound's ceiling, but they do
not guarantee a tighter bound or a better retriever [@poole2019variational].

The geometric view is often more useful in practice. On normalized vectors,
contrastive training rewards *alignment*, labeled positive pairs lying close
together, and *uniformity*, the overall representation distribution spreading
evenly over the sphere. Wang and Isola proved an asymptotic relationship under a
symmetric sampling model and showed these quantities were useful diagnostics on
their evaluated vision and language tasks [@wang2020alignment]. Query-document
retrieval can be asymmetric, so this is a diagnostic analogy rather than a
theorem about every dual encoder. SimCSE demonstrated the mechanism for sentence
similarity: dropout, which randomly zeroes some activations during a forward
pass, created two views of one sentence in its unsupervised setting, while
entailment and contradiction pairs supplied positives and hard negatives in its
supervised setting [@gao2021simcse]. The same paper explains why the objective
opens the cone. With negatives drawn from the data distribution, the uniformity
term upper-bounds the sum of the entries of the embedding Gram matrix, which bounds
its largest eigenvalue when the entries are positive, so minimizing the loss
flattens the singular-value spectrum of the embeddings instead of letting a few
directions dominate [@gao2021simcse].

Temperature controls how the loss distributes gradient across candidates. A
high-scoring negative receives more softmax mass and therefore a larger
gradient pushing its score down; the weight grows with $\exp(s/\tau)$, so the loss
is hardness-aware. As $\tau$ approaches zero nearly all of the gradient goes to the
single hardest negative and the loss approaches a margin loss, while a large
$\tau$ spreads the gradient evenly and ignores hardness [@wang2021behaviour].
Lowering $\tau$ concentrates relative weight on the highest-scoring negatives,
but it also amplifies mislabeled negatives and can destroy useful local
neighborhoods; Wang and Liu call this the uniformity-tolerance dilemma. There is no task-independent best temperature. Tune it together
with normalization, batch composition, duplicate masking, and the negative
miner; a numerical value copied from another model has no stable meaning when
the score scale changes.

The cell below trains a linear encoder with the in-batch loss above, on synthetic
texts whose raw features share one large offset and therefore start in a narrow
cone. It checks its analytic gradient, including the normalization step, against a
finite difference, then trains at six temperatures and tracks Wang and Isola's two
quantities on held-out pairs. The untrained cone scores well on alignment only
because every pair is close; training spreads the space and gives some alignment
back, and recall peaks at an intermediate temperature. Change the noise level in
`view` or the embedding size `k` and the best temperature moves, which is the sense
in which a temperature copied from another model has no stable meaning.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
K, D, k, B = 512, 32, 16, 64  # topics, raw feature size, embedding size, batch size
topics = rng.normal(size=(K, D))
offset = 4 * rng.normal(size=D)  # a shared direction: raw features start in a narrow cone
def view(ids):  # one noisy text about each topic, as raw features
    return topics[ids] + offset + 0.8 * rng.normal(size=(len(ids), D))

def loss_and_grad(W, X, Y, tau):
    """Mean in-batch InfoNCE on normalized embeddings, and its gradient in W."""
    zu, zv = X @ W, Y @ W
    nu, nv = np.linalg.norm(zu, axis=1, keepdims=True), np.linalg.norm(zv, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    u, v = zu / nu, zv / nv
    S = u @ v.T / tau
    P = np.exp(S - S.max(1, keepdims=True)); P /= P.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    dS = (P - np.eye(len(X))) / (len(X) * tau)  # softmax minus one-hot, per query
    gu, gv = dS @ v, dS.T @ u
    gzu, gzv = (gu - (gu * u).sum(1, keepdims=True) * u) / nu, (gv - (gv * v).sum(1, keepdims=True) * v) / nv
    return -np.mean(np.log(np.diag(P))), X.T @ gzu + Y.T @ gzv

def geometry(W, q, d):  # Wang and Isola's alignment and uniformity, plus recall@1
    u, v = [(x @ W) / np.linalg.norm(x @ W, axis=1, keepdims=True) for x in (q, d)]
    sq = 2 - 2 * (v @ v.T)[np.triu_indices(K, 1)]
    return np.mean(np.sum((u - v) ** 2, 1)), np.log(np.mean(np.exp(-2 * sq))), np.mean(np.argmax(u @ v.T, 1) == np.arange(K))

W0 = 0.3 * np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=(D, k))
X, Y = view(np.arange(B)), view(np.arange(B))
E = np.zeros_like(W0); E[3, 5] = 1e-6  # check the analytic gradient against a finite difference
fd = (loss_and_grad(W0 + E, X, Y, 0.1)[0] - loss_and_grad(W0 - E, X, Y, 0.1)[0]) / 2e-6
assert abs(fd - loss_and_grad(W0, X, Y, 0.1)[1][3, 5]) < 1e-6

q, d = view(np.arange(K)), view(np.arange(K))  # held-out queries and documents
start = geometry(W0, q, d)
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6))
taus, recall = [0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0], []
for tau in taus:
    W, path = W0.copy(), [start]
    for step in range(1, 401):
        ids = rng.choice(K, B, replace=False)
        g = loss_and_grad(W, view(ids), view(ids), tau)[1]
        W -= 0.05 * g / np.linalg.norm(g)  # normalized step, comparable across temperatures
        if step % 50 == 0:
            path.append(geometry(W, q, d))
    a, un, r = np.array(path).T
    assert un[-1] < un[0] and r[-1] > r[0], "training spreads the cone and improves recall"
    recall.append(r[-1])
    if tau in (0.05, 0.1, 1.0):
        ax1.plot(un, a, "o-", ms=3, label=f"τ = {tau}")
ax1.annotate("untrained", (start[1], start[0]), fontsize=8, ha="right", va="bottom")
ax1.set_xlabel("uniformity (lower = more spread)"); ax1.set_ylabel("alignment (lower = pairs closer)")
ax1.set_title("Training trades alignment for uniformity"); ax1.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax2.plot(taus, recall, "o-", color="0.3"); ax2.axhline(start[2], color="0.6", ls=":", lw=1)
ax2.set_xscale("log"); ax2.set_xlabel("temperature τ"); ax2.set_ylabel(f"recall@1 among {K} documents")
ax2.set_title(f"Best here: τ = {taus[int(np.argmax(recall))]}")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
::::

## Interaction placement fixes the cost envelope

The moment at which query and document tokens can interact determines what can
be precomputed.

| Architecture | Pair score | What can be indexed | Main cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dual encoder | one-vector inner product or cosine | one vector per document | loses token-level cross-attention |
| Late interaction | token-vector aggregation | document token vectors | larger index and more online scoring |
| Cross-encoder | joint transformer over the pair | no query-independent document score | one model pass per candidate pair |

A dual encoder is the usual first-stage dense retriever because the corpus side
is independent of the query. A cross-encoder is more expressive because it
reads the pair jointly, but that expressiveness does not guarantee the best
result on every workload. Its common production role is reranking a bounded
candidate set, where the number of pairwise passes is affordable. Sentence-BERT
put numbers on the gap: finding the most similar pair among 10,000 sentences with
a BERT cross-encoder takes about 50 million inference passes, roughly 65 hours,
and about 5 seconds when each sentence is encoded once by a siamese dual encoder
[@reimers2019sbert].

ColBERT occupies the middle. It encodes query and document tokens independently
and applies late interaction through MaxSim:

$$
S_{\mathrm{LI}}(q,d)
=\sum_{i=1}^{T_q}
\max_{1\le j\le T_d}
\widehat{q}_i^\mathsf{T}\widehat{d}_j.
$$

Here $T_q$ and $T_d$ are the query and document token counts, and
$\widehat{q}_i,\widehat{d}_j\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are normalized token vectors.
For each query token, MaxSim keeps the best document-token match and then sums
those matches. Document vectors remain precomputable, but the index stores many
vectors per document. ColBERTv2 reduced the footprint of an uncompressed
late-interaction index by six to ten times in its experiments through residual
compression and denoised supervision; that comparison was not against a
single-vector index [@santhanam2022colbertv2].

```{figure}
//| figure: interaction-cost
//| label: fig-embedding-interaction-cost
//| fig-cap: "Where query and document tokens meet, and what that placement fixes. A dual encoder pools each side into one vector and scores $u^\mathsf{T}v$; late interaction keeps one vector per token and adds up, over the query tokens, each one's best match among the document tokens, the MaxSim of $S_{\mathrm{LI}}$ (the similarities in the grid are illustrative); a cross-encoder reads the pair as one sequence. Dashed boxes mark what is computed before any query arrives. The rows count the resulting costs for a corpus of $N$ documents: the raw index payload $S_{\mathrm{raw}} = Ndb$, with one 768-coordinate vector per document or one 128-coordinate vector for each of $T_d = 128$ document tokens; document encoder passes before any query; encoder passes per query; and the multiply-adds of scoring every document by exact search or only $k$ reranked candidates, with $T_q = 32$ query tokens. Bar lengths compare the three scorers within each row. The sizes are illustrative."
```

## Training data defines relevance

What “related” means comes from the positive-pair policy, the rule for which
text pairs are labeled relevant; the loss only enforces the labels that policy
supplies. A search click, a question with an answer-bearing passage, two duplicate
records, a translation pair, and two sentences with similar meaning express
different relations. Combining them without task labels asks one vector space
to satisfy incompatible orderings. Every training row therefore needs the
query and document roles, task, languages, source and license, source version,
label origin and confidence, deduplication group, split assignment, and any
teacher or miner revision.

In-batch negatives reuse the other $B-1$ documents of the batch in the loss
above. In the $B\times B$ matrix of scores $s(u_i,v_j)$, the diagonal holds the
labeled pairs and each off-diagonal cell is treated as a negative. Dense Passage
Retrieval used this efficiently and added BM25-mined candidates in its
open-domain QA experiments, where it outperformed BM25 by 9 to 19 points of
absolute top-20 passage accuracy [@karpukhin2020dense]. Some reused documents are
relevant to the query: two batch rows may share a relevant document,
duplicate one another, or contain different valid answers to the same query.
Known positives and duplicate groups must be masked before the loss treats
off-diagonal cells as negatives. Larger batches add compute, communication, and
false-negative exposure as well as more candidates.

Once random negatives become easy, they stop teaching: a negative far from the
query receives almost no softmax weight, so its gradient nearly vanishes. A frozen
checkpoint can instead retrieve high-scoring unjudged documents from the corpus.
ANCE refreshed such an index asynchronously so the miner tracked the model over
training, and its dot-product retriever nearly matched BM25 retrieval followed by
BERT reranking while running about 100 times faster [@xiong2021ance]. RocketQA also
shared negatives across the devices of a data-parallel batch, so each query saw
many more candidates than one device holds [@qu2021rocketqa]. Those candidates
are *unjudged*, not known to be irrelevant. RocketQA reported that sparse labels
made many top retrieved passages false negatives and used a cross-encoder to
filter candidates [@qu2021rocketqa]. A teacher model of this kind, a stronger
scorer whose outputs become labels, is still fallible. Preserve known
positives, near duplicates, answer-bearing passages, and multi-positive labels;
send uncertain high-impact examples to human judgment rather than converting a
teacher score directly into truth.

```{figure}
//| figure: infonce-gradient
//| label: fig-embedding-infonce-gradient
//| fig-cap: "The in-batch loss $\mathcal{L}_i$ of one query on two-dimensional unit vectors, with 16 negatives at illustrative angles, 15 of them seeded and one fixed near the query. Scores are cosines, the bars are the softmax weights $p_j$ of $s_j/\tau$, and $\mathcal{L}_i = -\log p_+$. At the query, the arrows split the descent direction exactly, $-\tau\,\partial\mathcal{L}_i/\partial u = (1-p_+)(v_+ - u) + \sum_{j \ne +} p_j (u - v_j)$: a pull along the chord to the positive, and a push away from each negative weighted by its softmax share. Renormalizing $u$ keeps only the part of each term along the circle, which the panel on the movement of $u$ lists term by term. Hardness moves every negative toward the query by the same fraction of its angle, and a lower $\tau$ concentrates the weight, and with it the push, on the nearest negatives. With the toggle on, the nearest negative is a relevant document that the labels call negative: the larger its weight, the harder the loss pushes the query away from a correct answer."
```

Weak supervision, which takes labels from noisy automatic signals instead of
human judgment, expands positive coverage at the cost of label noise. Contriever
needed no labels at all: it took two random crops of one document as a positive
pair, kept negatives in a momentum queue so their number did not depend on the
batch, and outperformed BM25 on 11 of 15 BEIR datasets by recall@100
[@izacard2022contriever]. E5 filtered naturally occurring web pairs, such as
posts with their comments, questions with their answers, and titles with their
passages, before contrastive pretraining [@wang2022e5], and GTE and the BGE models
of C-Pack follow the same shape of large mined pretraining followed by a supervised
stage [@li2023gte; @xiao2023cpack]. Scaling the backbone was a separate lever:
Sentence-T5 and GTR took T5 encoders to billions of parameters and found that the
larger dual encoders generalized better out of domain [@ni2022sentencet5;
@ni2022gtr]. Later work generated diverse tasks and pairs with a language
model, then fine-tuned a decoder into the embedder on the synthetic data
[@wang2023e5mistral], and decoder-initialized embedders such as Gemini Embedding
and the open Qwen3 Embedding models continue that line [@lee2025gemini;
@zhang2025qwen3embedding]. Synthetic generation can cover rare intents and languages,
but it also copies the generator's factual errors, style, and task assumptions.
Keep prompts, generator revisions, filters, and source rights with the dataset.
Split by source and time before mining so near duplicates cannot leak across
train and evaluation.

Distillation, training one model to reproduce a stronger model's scores, is
another label source. A cross-encoder can score a bounded set of
query-document pairs, and the dual encoder can learn its pairwise margins rather
than its raw score scale, because the two architectures score on different scales;
Margin-MSE is that objective [@hofstatter2020marginmse]. TAS-B combined it with
topic-aware sampling, drawing each batch from one cluster of queries so the
in-batch negatives are topically hard, and trained a strong dense retriever on a
single consumer GPU [@hofstatter2021tasb]. Distillation inherits the teacher's bias and is limited
to the candidate set the teacher sees. It cannot teach a distinction that mining
never presents.

## One model can expose several contracts

General-purpose embedders often support task instructions. INSTRUCTOR trained a
single model across a large mixture by embedding each input with a description
of its task and domain [@su2022instructor]. FollowIR found that many tested
retrievers used detailed instructions largely as extra keywords, while targeted
fine-tuning improved constraint following [@weller2024followir]. Treat the exact
instruction template as a versioned part of the spec and test paraphrases,
negation, exclusions, and conflicting constraints.

Dimension can also be a trained interface. Matryoshka representation learning
attaches losses to selected vector prefixes, so that the first $m$ coordinates
of an embedding also work as a smaller embedding for each selected $m$. For a
retrieval adaptation, write

$$
z^{(m)}=
\frac{z_{1:m}}{\lVert z_{1:m}\rVert_2},
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MRL}}
=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}} c_m\,
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{(m)}.
$$

Here $z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the full embedding, $z_{1:m}$ is its first $m$
coordinates, $\mathcal{M}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ is the set of trained prefix
dimensions, $c_m\ge0$ is the weight for prefix $m$, and
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{(m)}$ applies the contrastive loss using
independently normalized $m$-dimensional query and document prefixes. Only
trained dimensions are promised. Slicing a normalized full vector does not leave
a normalized prefix, and arbitrary intermediate dimensions are not guaranteed to
work.

The original Matryoshka work learned coarse-to-fine representations across
vision and language evaluations and reported strong size and retrieval trade-offs
on its tested datasets [@kusupati2022matryoshka]. Its main systems benefit is one
model forward pass that can feed indexes of several supported dimensions. The
multiple training losses add training cost, and a shorter prefix is not always
strictly worse or always equal to a separately trained model. Measure
every offered dimension on the deployment workload.

## Indexes make compatibility operational

For $N$ stored vectors, dimension $d$, and $b$ bytes per coordinate, the raw
vector payload is

$$
S_{\mathrm{raw}} = N d b \quad\text{bytes}.
$$

Here $S_{\mathrm{raw}}$ excludes document metadata, graph or inverted-index
overhead, replicas, centroids, and temporary migration copies. Lower dimension,
reduced precision, product quantization, and late-interaction compression change
storage, memory bandwidth, latency, and neighbor recall in different ways. A
smaller payload is useful only if the resulting end-to-end retrieval quality is
still acceptable.

Changing any `EmbeddingSpec` field creates a new index generation. Do not
compare query vectors from one model with document vectors from another, even
when the dimensions match. Build the replacement beside the current index,
re-embed the complete authorized corpus, and dual-read representative traffic.
Compare exact vector rankings first, then the rankings of the approximate
nearest-neighbor (ANN) index, so representation drift is not confused with ANN
loss. Cut traffic over explicitly and retain a rollback window. Tombstones,
source updates, and ACL changes must reach every live generation and every
embedding cache.

Embeddings are derived content, not anonymized content. They inherit the source's
tenant, authorization, retention, residency, and deletion policy. A vector index
must not become a path around the authorization invariant in
@sec-rag-retrieval. Cache keys include the spec hash, input content hash, role,
instruction version, and tenant or other isolation boundary. Provider logs and
batching paths need the same data-handling review as any other model call.

## Evaluation must match the use

An aggregate embedding leaderboard is useful for screening candidates;
deployment selection needs evaluation on the target workload. MTEB demonstrated
that models which perform well on semantic textual similarity do not necessarily
dominate clustering, classification, reranking, and retrieval
[@muennighoff2022mteb]. MMTEB expanded the language and task coverage and showed
why a single English average is even less informative [@enevoldsen2025mmteb].
These benchmarks compare many workloads efficiently; they cannot reproduce a
private corpus, its permissions, its update pattern, or its exact definition of
relevance.

For a retrieval embedder, freeze the corpus version, chunking, query set,
relevance judgments, query and document roles, spec hash, and index parameters.
Then evaluate these boundaries separately:

- **Representation:** exact-search recall@k and nDCG@k, hard-negative error,
  calibration by score band, and performance against BM25 and the current model.
- **Approximation:** ANN recall against exact neighbors, empty-result rate,
  latency, memory, and index-build time at each compression or dimension setting.
- **Slices:** query intent, document source, length and truncation, language,
  script, cross-lingual direction, code switching, freshness, and permission
  cohort. Report the worst material slice as well as the mean.
- **Operations:** query encoding latency, document throughput, accelerator and
  CPU cost, raw and total index bytes, cache hit rate, generation age, migration
  duration, and rollback success.
- **End to end:** evidence recall after packing, answer quality, citation support,
  abstention, latency, and cost with the generator and reranker held fixed.

Use paired per-query comparisons and bootstrap confidence intervals. Include
queries with multiple valid passages and unanswerable queries. Perturb task
instructions, shorten and lengthen documents, add near duplicates, change a
fact, delete a source, revoke access, and shift the query language. A model with
the higher clean average is still the wrong production embedder if it fails
deletion, one language, or a high-value query cohort.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Whether one general embedding model can serve every task remains unsettled.
Shared training can transfer useful structure and simplify operations.
Instruction conditioning can expose several task-specific geometries through one
checkpoint. Yet symmetric similarity, asymmetric relevance, clustering, and
classification impose different neighborhoods. MTEB found no single method
dominated every task in its study, while later large and multilingual models
changed the frontier without removing that task dependence
[@muennighoff2022mteb; @enevoldsen2025mmteb]. On the evidence so far, model
choice is conditional on the task mixture, languages, corpus, and cost envelope
being measured. The size of the model settles less than it appears to: at the time
of the MMTEB study the
best publicly available model was a 560-million-parameter multilingual encoder,
ahead of decoder-based embedders an order of magnitude larger
[@enevoldsen2025mmteb], and BEIR found that dense retrievers of its time
generalized worse than BM25 outside their training domain [@thakur2021beir], so a
leaderboard won in distribution may not transfer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint
The scoring contract sets storage and serving costs. Dimension multiplies the
raw index payload; pooling and model size set encoding throughput; normalization
and similarity constrain the search primitive; late interaction multiplies the
number of stored vectors. These costs reach backward into training through
Matryoshka losses, distillation, quantization-aware evaluation, and the choice of
interaction architecture. They reach forward into the retrieval budgets and
index migrations of @sec-rag-retrieval.
:::

An embedder produces a versioned score under the scoring contract of one task.
Retrieval uses that score to select evidence and remains responsible for
authorization, freshness, fusion, and abstention. The next chapter,
@sec-context-engineering, starts after retrieval has selected evidence and asks
how instructions, history, tool results, and retrieved material should share a
bounded working context.
